title: Multigenerational Travel: Planning a Trip That Works for Ages 6 to 76
metaDescription: How to plan a trip across three generations — destination choice, accommodation, pacing, money and the conversations to have before you book.
excerpt: Three generations, one holiday, wildly different definitions of a good day. Here is how to plan one that nobody endures.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
Multigenerational trips are growing fast, for reasons that have little to do with travel trends: families are more dispersed, grandparents are more mobile and more willing to fund, and a shared holiday is often the only time three generations occupy the same space for more than a meal.

They are also the hardest trips to plan, because you are not designing for one group. You are designing for a six-year-old who needs a pool, a teenager who needs Wi-Fi and autonomy, parents who need a break from parenting, and grandparents who need a manageable pace and a proper bed.

The good news: the constraints are well understood, and most failures are predictable.

## The Conversations to Have Before Booking

Three questions, asked explicitly rather than assumed. Almost every multigenerational trip that goes wrong went wrong here.

**Who is paying for what?** The most common source of tension. Are grandparents covering accommodation? Is everyone paying their own flights? Are meals shared or separate? Ambiguity here curdles into resentment by day four. Settle it in one conversation, in plain terms, before anything is booked.

**What does everyone actually want?** Ask each person for one non-negotiable and one thing they would rather not do. You will learn that the grandparents dread a long transfer, the teenager will tolerate anything with decent Wi-Fi, and the eight-year-old only cares about the pool. This is enormously useful information and nobody volunteers it unprompted.

**How much time together is together enough?** The single biggest mistake in multigenerational travel is assuming everyone wants every meal and every activity as a unit. Most families want two or three shared moments a day and the rest flexible. Saying that out loud early removes the guilt from splitting up.

![Family Travel travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1591849995584-262878b2d556?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Choosing the Destination

Filter hard on four things:

**Flight length and time zone.** Long-haul with a large time difference is brutal for both young children and older travellers, and the recovery eats several days at each end. Under six hours and within three time zones is the sweet spot. If you must go long-haul, stay at least two weeks so the adjustment is worth it.

**Medical access.** Not pessimism, practicality. Somewhere with a decent hospital within a reasonable drive matters when the group includes small children and people in their seventies.

**Walkability and terrain.** Cobbled hill towns are beautiful and genuinely difficult with a pushchair or a knee replacement. Check whether the charming old town is on a hill before falling in love with it.

**Heat.** Very young and older travellers both handle extreme heat poorly. A Mediterranean August is a harder holiday than it looks.

Destinations that consistently work: Portugal's Algarve, Italy's Puglia and Tuscany, Spain's Costa Brava, Greece's larger islands, Thailand's Krabi and Hua Hin, Sri Lanka's south coast, Kerala, Goa outside peak, Bali's Sanur and Ubud, Costa Rica, and coastal Croatia.

## Accommodation Is the Decision That Matters Most

More than the destination. Three options, with clear trade-offs:

**A villa or large rental.** Usually the best answer. Shared living space means the group naturally gathers without forcing it, a kitchen removes the tyranny of every meal being a restaurant negotiation, and a pool solves the children entirely. Check the bedroom and bathroom configuration carefully — a "sleeps 10" villa with one bathroom is a difficult week.

**Adjoining hotel rooms or apartments.** More service, less togetherness. Works well when the group wants more independence, and when nobody wants to cook.

**A resort with a kids' club.** Expensive, and genuinely transformative for parents of young children. The kids are happy and supervised, the adults get actual rest, and the grandparents get time with the grandchildren on their own terms.

Non-negotiables to check regardless: **ground-floor or lift access** to at least one bedroom, **air conditioning**, **a bathroom situation that works**, and **reliable Wi-Fi** — which is not a teenage indulgence but the thing that makes a slow afternoon tolerable for half the group.

![Family Travel travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1602506272597-b44a3e67701e?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Pacing: The Two-Thirds Rule

Plan roughly two-thirds of what you would plan for a trip with your own generation only.

More specifically:

- **One main activity per day.** Not two. Not a morning thing and an afternoon thing.
- **Mornings for anything demanding.** Energy is highest and heat is lowest.
- **A genuine rest block in the afternoon.** Naps for the youngest, a book for the oldest, a swim for everyone in between.
- **At least one completely empty day** in a week. More on a longer trip.
- **Eat the main meal at lunch** if the group skews young or old. Late dinners are a European habit that does not suit either end of the age range.

## Build In Splitting Up

This is the technique that makes multigenerational trips work, and it needs to be planned rather than improvised.

Design days where the group naturally divides and reconvenes: the grandparents and small children go to the beach in the morning while the parents hike; the teenagers take the afternoon in town while everyone else rests; the adults get an evening out while the grandparents take the bedtime shift.

That last swap — an evening where the parents go to dinner alone — is often the single most valued thing in the entire holiday, for both generations.

Write these splits into the plan explicitly. When the itinerary says "morning: beach (grandparents + kids) / hike (everyone else)", nobody has to ask for permission or feel they are abandoning the group.

## Practical Details That Prevent Problems

- **Everyone's medication, in hand luggage, with a written list** of names, doses and prescribing details
- **Travel insurance that covers pre-existing conditions** for older travellers — and be aware that many policies have age limits
- **Copies of passports and insurance** shared with everyone, not just the organiser
- **Consent letters** if a grandparent is travelling with a grandchild without the parents
- **One shared plan everyone can see**, rather than one organiser holding it all
- **A clear money system** for shared costs

That last two points deserve emphasis. Multigenerational trips almost always have one organiser who holds the entire plan in their head and becomes the bottleneck for every question — which means they never get a holiday. Putting the itinerary somewhere everyone can read it independently, with shared expenses logged as they happen, is the difference between organising a trip and running one for a fortnight. **Trypinn** is built for exactly this: one plan, visible to the whole group, with the expense tracking alongside it.

## The Thing Worth Remembering

These trips are rarely about the destination. Nobody remembers which beach it was. They remember the grandfather teaching a seven-year-old to play cards, the evening everyone ate outside and nobody looked at a phone, the photograph with all three generations in it.

Plan for those moments — which means planning fewer other things — and the trip works almost regardless of where you go.
